idea: Basic plumbing maintenance every homeowner should know
title: Servicing a Clogged Faucet Aerator
description: Learn how faucet aerators trap debris, why water flow drops while static pipe pressure remains unchanged, and how to safely disassemble and clean the screen assembly to restore proper fixture volume.
image_prompt: Photorealistic vertical 9:16 macro photograph of a modern chrome basin faucet with its front aerator assembly unscrewed and neatly laid out in sequence on a clean countertop near the sink rim. The components are displayed clearly in disassembly order: the chrome threaded housing, a black rubber flat sealing washer, a fine stainless steel mesh screen with light mineral debris, and a plastic flow restrictor core. Natural morning window lighting highlights the metal threads and internal components. The scene is clean and professional. The main subject is centered in the middle and lower portion of the image, leaving clean negative space at the top. Physically accurate thread geometry and realistic plumbing materials. No text, no logos, no watermarks, no labels, no fake product branding.
visual_story: The visual displays the internal component sequence of a standard faucet aerator immediately after removal from the spout tip. Viewers can see how mineral flakes and pipe debris settle on top of the fine mesh screen, restricting water flow volume while static water pressure in the branch line remains unaffected. Seeing the exact layering—housing, rubber washer, mesh screen, flow regulator—helps homeowners and apprentices understand how to disassemble, clean, and reassemble the unit without damaging fine brass threads.

on_image_text.hook: Low Faucet Flow? Check the Aerator First
on_image_text.explanation: Sediment collects at the spout screen, choking flow volume even when pipe pressure is normal.
on_image_text.takeaway: Unscrew counter-clockwise, rinse internal screens clean, and hand-tighten to restore volume.
